name: AKU's 18th National Health Sciences Research Symposium discusses ways to fight cancer

content.text: There was also a call for cancer registries, which will make the task of keeping track of cancer cases easier and eventually assist in developing a national cancer control programme.
The three-day event played host to health experts from around the world and presented a valuable insight into various aspects of the disease nationally, and in South Asia.

Inaugurating the session, Dr Salman Naseem Adil, Chair, Organising Committee, NHSRS and Associate Professor, Department of Oncology, AKU warned that the incidence of cancer is likely to grow. According to the World Health Organization, the number of new cases will rise by approximately 70 per cent in the next two decades, with almost two-thirds of annual cases in Asia, Africa, and Central and South America. This makes it essential for the medical world to stay abreast with cancer-related issues in order to counter the disease successfully.

Discussing preventive measures, Dr Malcolm Moore, Head, Union for International Cancer Control, Asia Regional Office, Korea, underlined the need to adopt a healthier lifestyle and diet. Comparing cancer statistics across South Asia, he pointed out that, in Pakistan, due to smoking, nutritional and hormonal factors, lung cancer may be on the rise. In Karachi, the ratio of lung cancer in men and women is 4.8:1 and 2.6:1 respectively. Breast cancer was also found to be highly prevalent in women that is almost 31 per cent.

In the developed world, cancer registries offer an unbiased profile of the disease and provide the reliable population-based information needed to develop country cancer control plans. Ms Uzma Rizwan, Director, Cancer Data Center and Accreditation, CarePoint Health, USA, explained the types of cancer registries available and how they could serve as a model for Pakistan. "Data collection is important, but to use the data is far more important," she added.
At the workshops, experts spoke about different types of cancer, their prevalence in Pakistan and some simple preventive measures.

Approximately one in every 8-10 women in Pakistan suffers from breast cancer, pointed out Dr Abida Sattar, Assistant Professor, Department of Surgery, AKU. "Early detection can make a lot of difference" and signs such as a breast or armpit lump, breast retraction or skin changes should not be ignored. Dr Sattar suggested that women over 35 years should have a 'baseline' mammogram followed by a routine mammogram every year.

"Cancer of the mouth, throat, lungs and food pipe is 10 times more prevalent than all other cancers," said Dr Javaid A Khan, Professor, Department of Medicine, AKU. Tobacco is the cause of almost 40 per cent of cancer in men in Pakistan and he blamed the non-implementation of anti-smoking and anti-tobacco laws in public places for this high rate.

Dr Zehra Fadoo, Associate Professor, Department of Oncology, AKU highlighted the fact that there were about 8,000 children under 18 in Pakistan suffering from cancer. Putting the onus on the limited number of paediatric oncology centres, she added: "Lack of access to good quality medical advice, early diagnosis, timely treatment and care and lack of essential medications are really the reasons why children with cancer in developing countries often do not survive."

Nursing care is equally important and "nurses' involvement in survivorship helps patients live their life better," said Ms Rehana Elahi, Shaukat Khanum Memorial Cancer Hospital and Research Centre, Lahore. She spoke of the pivotal role that nurses play in cancer patients' interaction with the hospital. Their intervention and oversight of patient care as well as coordinating with other health professionals is valuable input in helping patients manage and live with their illness.
The second day of the symposium brought further nuggets of medical wisdom on cancer with focus on research as the key to preventive and treatment strategies.

Dr Ikram Burney, Consultant Oncologist at Sultan Qaboos University Hospital, Oman, compared hospitals active in research with those that are inactive. Quoting a study involving 165 hospitals, he concluded that the 80 hospitals involved in research provided better care to their patients -with improved processes of care, training, education and specialisation.

Touching upon the common cancer myths and misconceptions, Dr Adnan Jabbar, Assistant Professor, Department of Oncology, AKU reiterated the need for cancer screening adding that a lot of lives can be saved by this single measure. "Just three factors can increase the chances of cancer survival - early detection, improved treatment and access to care, and identified habits that put people at risk of getting cancer," Dr Jabbar added.

Once cancer is detected and treated, an essential part of treatment should be to manage pain. Dr Gauhar Afshan, Professor and Chairman, Department of Anaesthesiology, AKU said that 5.5 million people worldwide receive no treatment or minimal assistance for their cancer pain even though, "pain is among the most common and feared symptoms in cancer patients". Outlining the barriers to managing cancer pain in developing countries, she said that pain is generally regarded as part of cancer treatment and patients are encouraged to live with it rather than to actively take steps to manage it. "This is an attitude that needs to change and be part of the counseling provided to patients and their families," she emphasised.

Focusing on the oft-neglected topic of good nutrition in cancer care, Bushra Mushtaq, Senior Dietician, AKUH talked about how healthy eating habits, planned and monitored by a qualified dietician, can help a patient deal with the effects of cancer and its treatment. Quoting a study, she said that once or twice a month consultation with a dietitian helped cancer patients improve their protein intake by around 239kcal per day as compared to a group that was not counseled, helping improve recovery and quality of life.

Experts also discussed different cancers and progress in treatment. Lung cancer is not only the leading form of cancer globally; it also has the highest mortality rate with 90 per cent of patients dying of it. Taking this further, Dr Ghulam Haider of Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre, Karachi, reiterated the need for early detection - there is 49 per cent chance of survival  when the disease is diagnosed at an early stage falling to a very low, 0-3 per cent at the advanced stage.

For a patient, a family history of cancer can make a huge difference. Familial breast cancer, for instance, accounts for 25 percent of cases. Dr Salman Kirmani, Associate Professor and Chair Department of Paediatrics and Child Health, AKU explained the utility of genetic testing which helps identify faulty genes in individuals in affected families. He advised that people should closely track their family medical history up to three generations. They should also keep tabs on any multiple tumors, recurrence and rare types of tumors and look for any patterns that may give a clue.

Dr Ather Kazmi of Shaukat Khanum Memorial Cancer Hospital and Research Centre, Lahore, outlined several different strategies and surgical practices to treat gastric cancer, the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths. "More than half the cases occur in East Asia, where Korea and Japan show the highest incidences," he added. He also explored the role of radiation in cancer survival and whether it improves the outcome of localised resectable gastric cancer.

Dr Farhat Abbas, Dean, Medical College, AKU spoke about prostate and bladder cancer. Despite being a common form of cancer in Pakistan (8.9 per cent in both men and women), patients of urinary bladder cancer present their cases at an advanced stage, he said. Dr Abbas also presented highlights from AKU's research in the area, concluding "molecular diagnosis of prostate and urinary bladder cancer is emerging as a promising tool with many potential benefits."

Panelists also discussed head and neck cancer with a focus on salivary gland tumors, oral cavity cancers and larynx/hypopharynx cancer. They reiterated the call for health services infrastructure and human resources to help combat this disease. "The silent nature of this form of the disease, misinterpretation of symptoms and lack of awareness about risk factors contribute to the delay in seeking treatment for patients' part," added Dr Shabbir Akhtar, Assistant Professor, Department of Surgery, AKU, who moderated the session.

Other key speakers on both the days included Dr Asim F. Belgaumi, Dr Faisal Dar, Dr Manzoor Hasan Zaidi, Dr Tazeen Ali, Dr Naureen Mushtaq, Dr Najeeb Naimatullah, Dr Muzaffar H. Qazilbash from USA, Dr Farrok Karsan, Dr Shaista Khan, Dr Tahir Shamsi, Dr Humayon Bashir, Dr Shahryar Noordin, Dr Keithe Cash, Dr Aasim Ahmed, Latif Sheikh, Dr Inam Pal, Dr Tayyaba Ansari, Dr Saulat Fatmi, Dr Aliya Aziz, Dr Abdus Samad and Dr Nadeem Pervez from UAE, among others.
In order to spread awareness about cancer a public awareness session was also conducted a day prior to the symposium.

content.title: AKU's 18th National Health Sciences Research Symposium discusses ways to fight cancer
content.author: Iqra Paintern
content.description: Adopt a healthy lifestyle and engage in preventive care to reduce your cancer risk said speakers at the Aga Khan University's 18th National Health Sciences Research Symposium on cancer and promoting comprehensive care.
